items.title: How Does Local Hardware Help Avoid Recurring Subscription Costs?
items.summary:
Cloud AI bills can add up fast.

In this short, Keiji Kamigusa explains how local hardware can help developers avoid recurring subscription costs by running AI models directly on a Mac they already own.

Instead of paying every month for every experiment, prompt, document workflow, or API call, local AI lets you build and test private chatbots, RAG apps, voice tools, and other AI-powered projects on your own machine.

That doesn’t mean cloud AI goes away. It means you get options: use the cloud when it makes sense, and use local models when privacy, control, or long-term cost matters more.

Build Applications with Local AI Models on a Mac shows you how to turn your Mac into a practical local AI development environment.

Learn more: https://hubs.la/Q04mY6wQ0

items.title: BREAKING: Google Hardwires Gemini Into Silicon to Tackle Compute Shortage
items.summary:
Google is developing Frozen V2, a custom AI chip that hardwires parts of Gemini's architecture directly into hardware. Unlike today's general-purpose TPUs that load models into memory and shuttle data back and forth, Frozen V2 bakes the neural network blueprint into the silicon itself. This reduces calculations and data travel, potentially serving 6 to 10 times more AI tokens per unit of power compared to Google's newest TPUs.

✅ Cypher 2026: Join 5,000+ AI leaders. Book now → https://cypher.analyticsindiamag.com/tickets
✅ Chess League: Test your skills → https://chess.analyticsindiamag.com/

The original concept from Google DeepMind's Jeff Dean locked in actual model weights, but that approach would have tied the chip to a single Gemini release. Frozen V2 is more flexible. It hardwires the underlying blueprint but lets engineers load new weights as needed. Google is dealing with a serious internal AI compute shortage, reportedly even paying SpaceX close to a billion dollars monthly to help bridge that gap. Frozen V2 is meant to ease that pressure by squeezing more useful AI output from hardware Google already has. Deployment is targeted for 2028. Paytm's board made a counterintuitive call after delivering blockbuster Q1 results. With consolidated net profit up 78.8% year-on-year to ₹222 crore and operating revenue growing 27.6% to ₹2,448 crore, investors expected a bonus share announcement. Instead, the board rejected it. The board's reasoning was direct: in a company that only recently turned consistently profitable, capital discipline matters more than a stock price sugar rush.

The company approved an additional ₹100 crore investment in wholly-owned subsidiary Paytm Money to fuel technology and regulatory capital needs. It also asked shareholders to extend the deadline for deploying leftover IPO funds to March 2029, reallocating capital toward core payments and strengthening the finserve ecosystem. In a leadership update, Google Search's former SVP Amitabh Kumar Singh joined as a non-executive director.
